United Church — Un homme, une communauté: United Church — One Man, One Community, One Story
Le fidèle Colin Forde dans le sanctuaire: Congregant Colin Forde in the sanctuary of United Church. Photo: Ahmed El Moudden
Le soleil s’est déjà couché lorsque nous: The sun has already set when we come out of the Lionel-Groulx metro station. Congregant Colin Forde is waiting for us in front of Union United Church, the first Black church in the country. There, we discover a little-known, rich and fascinating history. At the corner of Atwater Avenue and Delisle Street stands the imposing Saint-Irénée Catholic church, more than a century old. Right across from it, in its shadow, sits the small Union United Church, a Protestant church built at the same time. In this unequal coexistence, the story of the oldest Black church in Canada is already taking shape.
Arrivé au Canada il y a 35 ans de la Bar: Colin arrived in Canada from Barbados 35 years ago, and he has not always followed the path he is on today. Before, his life was steeped in “wine, women and song.” After a life of rock and reggae, rubbing shoulders with the Rolling Stones and reggae singer Peter Tosh, among others, Colin Forde, who was a hotel manager, changed course when he arrived in Canada. “I went through the $50,000 Rolex and the $30,000 bracelet, among other things; I lived it, and I realized it was vanity, nothing but vanity, and that it led nowhere,” he tells us wisely. His path changed radically after a heart attack. “I was on the operating table for eight hours, and they brought me back to life, thanks be to God,” says the longtime churchgoer. That moment brought him closer to his faith. After this ordeal, Colin went through deep introspection. “I decided to change my life, like Saul on the road to Damascus. I started to shed my self,” says Colin Forde, his hand on his heart.
Il se met à jouer avec la bague qu’il po: He begins to play with the skull-shaped ring he wears on his left middle finger. For Colin, this silver ring, given to him by Keith Richards of the Rolling Stones at a meeting in Jamaica, has become a symbol of the fragility and vulnerability of life. As for his beret, it is a symbol of the revolution led by the Black Panthers in the 1960s. “I wear it because I am against oppression, like my brothers who fought for me and with me,” the activist explains proudly. Now retired, he worked for more than 30 years in a textile factory in Montréal’s Chabanel district. “They worked me to death for nothing,” he says of the simplicity of his former job. “But you can’t catch blessings with a closed fist. You have to bloom where you are planted and say to the Lord: ‘Thank you for the small mercies,’” he professes with a smile full of grace, pointing a finger toward the sky.
L’espoir n’est pas toujours facile à cul: Hope is not always easy to cultivate for Colin, who has watched Quebec society change over the last 35 years. He tells us about his first experience in the job market, with his late friend Rudy. The two went to Chabanel Street to apply for a job. “We filled out the forms and gave them to the receptionist.” Five minutes later, at the bottom of the building, Rudy realized he had forgotten to write down his phone number. He went back up with Colin and asked the same receptionist if he could have his form back to add his contact information. “She went digging in the garbage and pulled out a crumpled piece of paper for him,” Colin recalls. “It’s not her, it’s the company’s behaviour; it’s a good thing we didn’t get that job because it would have been horrible,” Colin told his friend Rudy at the time. Unfortunately, it was neither the first nor the last experience of its kind that Colin has faced. He is all too familiar with white people clutching their purses when he walks behind them, or getting up when he sits next to them on the metro. “Even worse, I’ve seen dogs that only bark when they see Black people, never at white people!” He forcefully denounces the fact that “animals are treated better than Black people.” Today, Colin believes that racism in Canada is no less serious than in the United States. “There was a lot of racism in Canada, and we like to downplay it because we think we are morally ahead of the United States – there was a lot of racism and there still is, let’s say it, but people sweep it under the rug because they are too ashamed to admit what they did. Now we’ve gone from racism to fear, because people, white people, think we are going to do to them what they did to us,” says the septuagenarian.
Cet esprit révolutionnaire qui anime Col: This revolutionary spirit that drives Colin Forde also marks the history of the church where he welcomes us, which was founded by the Coloured Women’s Club in 1907. At the time, the Coloured Women’s Club was made up of seven Afro-Canadian women whose husbands worked as railway porters. As many African American slaves fleeing the United States came to settle in Canada, the need for a place of worship of their own was increasingly felt. “Being told to sit at the back of the church, then being ordered by the entire white congregation not to come back at the end of the service was the norm back then,” Colin explains. He sits on the church’s board of directors.
Ce type de discrimination est à l’origin: This type of discrimination is at the origin of the founding of Union United Church, which still campaigns for an inclusive future. Among the church’s efforts are the annual visits it organizes to the historic site N***** Rock, two hours from Montréal. It is where many African American and Afro-Canadian slaves, forced to relocate by the British Loyalists and settled in Canada, were buried. The graves are still unmarked. “Before the pandemic, we did historical tours during which there was a service,” Colin explains before singing the opening of Ride On King Jesus.
Alors que nous sommes assis au sous-sol,: As we sit in the basement, a dull thud echoes through the hall, which once rang with the piano notes of the famous pianist Oscar Peterson. Unsettled, we joke about blaming ghosts and spirits. We go up to the second floor, where another piece of the history of Black slavery in Canada is tucked away. A large tapestry reproduces the codes and symbols African American slaves used to communicate the routes that could guide them to the Underground Railroad and lead them to passage into Canada.
Au troisième étage, on découvre la salle: On the third floor, we discover the Nelson Mandela room. This is where the church’s administrative meetings are held. One image in particular shows a smiling Nelson Mandela, hands in the air, surrounded by members of the Montréal congregation. Recalling that visit in 1990, Colin lets all his admiration for South Africa’s first president show. “He gave off a different energy and different vibrations.” As he shows us around the sanctuary, he points to a large wooden cross above the pulpit. “It was under this cross that Nelson Mandela came to speak to the community about the mission of the African National Congress,” Colin Forde tells us proudly, adding that it is the only church in the country that Mandela visited after his release from prison. “There were so many people that they had to close off the neighbourhood.” Nelson Mandela, Desmond Tutu, Angela Davis, Oliver Jones, Oscar Peterson, Mathilda May and Anne Greenup are some of the historical figures and personalities who have climbed the steps of this small church.

<strong>Un héritage difficile à préserve: A legacy that is hard to preserve
À travers ses sculptures, ses photos, sa: Through its sculptures, photos and porcelain, the church keeps the past alive to create a better future. Dozens of images of plays, men’s groups, potluck meals, golf outings and former pastors tell the story of the place. At its peak, Union United Church was a social hub that nurtured a sense of belonging. “Many members of the congregation are from immigrant backgrounds, and joining the church was a first step in their process of integration,” Colin Forde explains. The church offers a “place where you can come and feel comfortable because you see people like you; you are represented.” He elaborates. “When you arrive here (in Quebec), it can be a cold, hard and lonely place; if you don’t have a good support system, you will wither on the vine.”
Un cliché en noir et blanc immortalise u: A black-and-white photograph immortalizes about sixty children in identical outfits: white top, black skirt and Ankara-print scarf. The image bears witness to a former reality. These days, young people are missing. Colin points to several causes that, in his view, explain this. First, he feels young people are not listened to enough. “Very often, young people are repressed. They live with a lot of worries and uncertainties, but they are not free to express themselves.” He goes on to say that technological progress encourages young people’s isolation. “Cell phones, television… families don’t spend much time together anymore.” He continues passionately: “There aren’t enough conversations between the older and younger generations. Young people don’t know their history, they don’t realize they are living on the blood, sweat and tears of those who came before them.”
Aujourd’hui, le vieillissement des membr: Today, the ageing of the congregation is changing the sense of community as it once existed. In the past, through its community activities (theatre, music, golf, etc.) and its services (soup kitchen and financial support for people in need), Union United Church made sure its members were taken care of. These days, the institution can no longer afford to do so. Since most members of the congregation are retirees, they can no longer contribute as much to the church’s finances. Colin explains that the pensions seniors receive barely allow them to feed themselves and buy their medication. He longs to bring back the church of the past, the one that was full of young people and often hosted social and cultural activities. To do so, he proposes listening more closely to young people and giving them the space they need to express themselves, but the church’s limited resources make this impossible. When asked what he would say to politicians if he could speak to them, he launches into a striking monologue: “I would tell them to come see us. They can’t know the needs of the people if they just stay in their houses in Westmount.”
Comme Colin le répète tout au long de la: As Colin repeats throughout the evening, “the flesh alone did not bring me here,” but also the support of his faith and his community. “That’s why we must invest in our own communities, because they are the way forward. We are going to leave this earth one day, and we must leave the world in better shape than we found it.” In his view, we need to learn to live in a more humane way, more oriented toward others. “People won’t remember what you gave them, but how you made them feel.” History is written into the very core of this congregation, but it is often overlooked in the public consciousness. “The things that were done to us should have made us disappear, wiped us off the map, but we are still here fighting, struggling, serving God and seeing the fruits of our labour… If a society tries to silence you, your voice will last forever,” concludes Colin Forde.
